segments.narration: Five hundred men worked fifteen years to build one hill. Silbury, in Wiltshire, stands thirty-nine metres high and holds 248,000 cubic metres of chalk.
That is eighteen million estimated man-hours, around 2400 BC. And almost no prehistoric artefacts have ever come out of it.
So people dug in anyway. A duke sank a shaft from the summit in 1776, and tunnels followed in 1849 and 1968.
The core gave up clay, flints, turf, antler tines and ox bones. Then in 2002 that 1776 shaft collapsed in heavy rain.
English Heritage backfilled the tunnels in 2007. Jim Leary and David Field concluded the point was never the finished mound, but the building of it.

verdicts.claim: Archaeologists estimate 18 million man-hours, equivalent to 500 men working 15 years; it was built between about 2400 and 2300 BC, and few prehistoric artefacts have been found in it.

verdicts.claim: Cornish miners overseen by the Duke of Northumberland sank a vertical shaft from the summit in October 1776, a horizontal tunnel was dug in 1849, and Richard Atkinson excavated from 1968 to 1970.
verdicts.note: 94% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The mound's core holds clay, flints, turf, gravel, shells, sarsen stones, ox bones and antler tines, and the 1776 shaft collapsed after heavy rain in May 2002.
verdicts.note: 89% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: English Heritage filled the old tunnels and shafts with chalk in 2007-2008, and Jim Leary and David Field concluded in 2010 that the purpose cannot be known and the building process may have mattered more than the finished hill.
